Chapter 30

The gallery

The sort lives in the URL; await in an {#each} with batched counts; a preview that opens with preloadData and a shallow goto without leaving, in a native modal <dialog>; crossfade between a card and the dialog; and a delete form per card with remove.for(id) and an optimistic override.

By the end of this chapter

Build a list page with async Svelte, preview a route without navigating to it, and delete optimistically with a per-item form.

The sort is read from page.url.searchParams, so a sorted gallery is a link: /gallery?sort=loved. Looking the value up in sorts does two jobs at once: an unknown ?sort= falls back to "new", and what comes out is a Sort, typed by the list it was found in, where a check followed by wanted as Sort would have been a cast. The chips are links to resolve("/(app)/gallery?sort=…") — SvelteKit navigates, page.url changes, the derived recomputes, and the query below re-runs with a new argument. No state, no handler.

Two awaits in one {#each}: the list, and each card’s counts. Every await getCounts(published.id) in this render is one batched request (ch. 23). The boundary shows the pending snippet until the list is in, and because the page is server-rendered, that snippet appears only on a client-side navigation with a cold cache. If getPatterns fails, the failed snippet shows the server’s sentence: what a boundary is handed has been through handleError already and is the App.Error itself, so it is error.message — no body in between (ch. 24 has the other shape).

Preview without leaving

href is resolve()d once and handed to both preloadData and goto, so the address that is preloaded is the address that is shown; the route id is checked at build time like every other link (ch. 27).

Why preloadData and then a shallow goto

On a wide screen, clicking a card opens it in a dialog rather than navigating away. preloadData(href) runs the pattern page’s load — which calls getPattern and warms its cache — and goto(href, { shallow: true, state: { preview } }) then changes the URL to the pattern’s address with the id in history state, *without* rendering the pattern page. Reload, and the real page appears at that URL; press back, and the dialog closes. On a phone, or with a modifier key held, the link is a link. This is shallow routing again (ch. 18), with a URL this time — and SvelteKit 3 keeps the two URLs apart: page.url still says /gallery, which is what the sort chips read, and page.shallow.url is the address in the bar.

Why a native <dialog> and showModal()

The preview covers the page and nothing behind it is any use while it is open, so it is *modal* — and modal is a set of promises a <div role="dialog"> has to fake one by one: focus moves inside when it opens, Tab cannot reach the page underneath, Escape closes it, focus goes back to whatever opened it, and assistive technology is told the rest of the page is out of reach. dialog.showModal() makes every one of those true. The browser puts the dialog in the top layer — above everything, so it needs no z-index — makes the rest of the document inert, and draws a ::backdrop behind it. This page used a <div> and kept none of the promises: a keyboard user who opened a card with Enter was left focused on the card behind the overlay, and Tab walked on into the gallery. The call is an attachment because “call a method on the element once it exists, and undo it when it goes” is exactly what an attachment is for; its teardown, close(), runs after the fade-out, and that is when the browser hands focus back to the card. The sound panel is the contrast: deliberately not modal, and a different element (ch. 18).

The dialog reads page.state.preview and calls getPattern(id) — cached by the preload — inside its own boundary. The id is {const id = $derived(page.state.preview)}. The {#if} asks only *whether* there is a preview, so nothing ties the block’s life to *which* one: a plain declaration would be right only for as long as nothing ever changed the id without closing the dialog first, and $derived makes that a question nobody has to answer (ch. 16). Escape closes a modal dialog by itself, and onclose turns that into history.back(), the same step the Close button and the back gesture take. A click whose target is the <dialog> element itself landed on its ::backdrop — everything inside is wrapped in .preview__body — and closes it too.

“Open the full page” is a plain link to resolve("/(app)/p/[id]", { id }) — the address already in the bar. In SvelteKit 3 a click on a link to the current address is not a no-op: it leaves shallow routing, replaces the preview’s history entry with a real navigation to the page, and refreshes. So back from the full page is the gallery, and the navigation is client-side; the gallery test checks both, with a marker on window that a document load would wipe. The same thing from a script is goto(page.shallow.url) — page.shallow describes the address in the bar while shallow routing is active, and goto without shallow: true is how you go there for real.

This link used to carry data-sveltekit-reload, which forces a document load, on the grounds that a client-side navigation to the same URL did nothing. That was SvelteKit 2’s behaviour. Under SvelteKit 3 the attribute only threw away the client-side navigation and cost a full reload.

Crossfade

crossfade returns a pair of transitions. An element leaving with out:send and another entering with in:receive under the same key are animated as one thing moving between two places — here, the card’s picture travelling into the dialog and back. The card renders its picture through the grid snippet with {#if page.state.preview !== published.id}, so opening the preview *removes* the card’s picture (send) as the dialog’s appears (receive). When there is no partner, fallback fades. The durations are functions rather than numbers, asked each time a transition starts, and they answer zero to anybody who asked for reduced motion. That has to be done here: Svelte plays its transitions through the Web Animations API, element.animate, and the stylesheet’s prefers-reduced-motion rule — which shortens every CSS transition and animation in the app — cannot touch those.

Yours, with a delete per card

remove.for(mine.id) gives each card its own instance of the form, so a pending delete disables *its* button and no other. It is a plain declaration, worked out once per row, and here that is right: the row is keyed by mine.id, so its id cannot change while the row exists. The enhance callback submits with .updates(getMine().withOverride(list => list.filter(...))): the card disappears before the server has answered, and comes back if the server refuses — with the refusal in the toast. submit() resolves to a boolean, false for a submission the schema refused before anything was sent, and “Deleted” is announced only for true. A second tab that still shows a card this one has deleted gets “Not yours, or not there”, the server’s own error(404, …), read from body.message by messageOf (ch. 24). The id travels as a hidden field, so with JavaScript off the same form still posts and the server still checks ownership.

One boundary around this section, not two, and the comment says why. There used to be a second boundary inside it, around the list, for a “Loading yours…” line. On a full page load that inner boundary hydrated its markup and never ran its effects — no attachments, so the delete forms were never enhanced, and Delete fell back to the plain POST that works with JavaScript off. It still deleted, which is why the suite did not notice; it only showed when a refused delete arrived as an error page instead of a toast. Taking away either the inner boundary or the batched await getCounts inside it was enough to bring the forms back, which points at that combination during hydration rather than at anything the page’s own code does. The inner boundary went, because the outer one already waits for everything in it. There is no upstream issue for it yet, because a report needs the fault reduced to a page without this app around it, and that work is not done; until it is, the condition for putting the inner boundary back is written in the file — the end-to-end test that deletes from two tabs (ch. 38) passing with it in place.

Checkpoint

  • You can say what preloadData returns and why the code checks result.type.
  • You can explain what send and receive need in common to animate as one element.
  • You can list what showModal() does that a <div role="dialog"> does not.
  • You can say why remove.for(id) exists rather than one shared remove form.
  • You can say what a refused delete looks like with the form enhanced, and without.
